newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BA faces trouble in air and on ground.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BA faces trouble in air and on ground.

text.p: The spectre of summer strike action loomed large over British Airways Plc on Wednesday after cabin crew voted for industrial action to settle a bitter five-month row over pay and conditions.
British Airways, fresh from a 60 million pound ($100.1 million) image makeover and anxiously seeking to seal a key alliance with American Airlines, could also face trouble on the ground.
Some 9,000 ground staff will vote next week whether to strike over the controversial sale of BA's long-haul catering business at London's busy Heathrow airport.

The sell-off and pay restructuring are part of the airline's business efficiency programme, aimed at saving one billion pounds by the turn of the century and securing BA's future in the cut-throat aviation business.
BA's new pay structure, estimated to save around 42 million pounds, has already been passed by the Cabin Crew 89 union, which represents around a quarter of cabin crew.

But the larger T&G union, representing almost three quarters of BA's mainline cabin crew, has baulked at the pay restructuring and condemned the cost of BA's new makeover while the airline was trying to slash costs elsewhere.
On Wednesday, the T&G said its members had clearly backed strike action. Some 75 percent of 9,000 cabin staff balloted took part in the vote. Of those, 73 percent favoured striking.
The union said it would decide on Monday what type of action to take, alarming investors who sent BA's shares down 14 pence to 686-1/2p.

BA's chief executive Bob Ayling said at a news conference he was convinced BA employees did not want to strike. He slammed the T&G union, saying it had "misled" and was putting pressure on its members.
"We will not be held back by 1970s-style trade unionism," Ayling said, pledging to keep BA flying and saying contingency plans were already in place.
Ayling said the union had quit the talks without explanation. He said the union had said the pay and conditions package was not at issue.
But T&G official Eddie McDermott said his union was unhappy with the deal and that BA had struck a secret agreement with the Cabin Crew 89 union and presented it as a fait accompli.

BA agreed a deal with Cabin Crew 89 comprising a basic wage rise of between 14.2 percent and 24 percent, with higher pensionable salaries and better profit-sharing terms, sickness and maternity leave benefits.

McDermott was scathing about BA's strike contingency plans, which include training senior staff to perform other tasks and drafting in new personnel to fill strikers' jobs. He said the creation of a "scab army" would harm services.

Ayling insisted BA would be able to maintain services if it came to a strike, noting that its European and domestic services from London's Gatwick airport and services operated by British Airways Regional from the UK regions were not involved in the ballot.
He made no mention of Heathrow, London's major hub, and said he could not say what impact a cabin crew strike could have.

Analysts played down the imminent threat of strike action, noting that BA had a buffer period because unions must give seven days' notice ahead of any strike action, which must be taken within 24 days of the ballot. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 4017 ($ = 0.599 British Pounds)
